findings.headline: Large accountable-body capital programmes (externally delivered schemes) adding £49.451m outturn
findings.detail: In addition to direct delivery, the council managed £49.451m of accountable-body schemes (projects delivered through external bodies like Combined Authorities or regional funds) that accelerated and reprofiled significantly: £3.935m accelerated from 2025/26, then £2.330m reprofiled out. The volatility suggests external partners' delivery constraints affect programme timing.
findings.matters: Reliance on external delivery creates exposure to third-party project delays and funding conditions outside direct council control.
findings.figures: Accountable Body Schemes Outturn 2025/26: £49.451m (vs approved £23.982m for direct delivery component). Accelerated £3.935m, then net virements out £2.330m.

findings.headline: £65.139m in additional capital investments added mid-year in February 2026
findings.detail: February 2026 Council meeting approved substantial additional capital investments totalling £65.139m, split across the multi-year programme. This followed approved schemes and came with offsetting project changes of (£4.426m). The scale suggests either a material reappraisal of capital priorities or new funding opportunity identified mid-year.
findings.matters: Mid-year addition of this scale indicates either unbudgeted capital needs or a change in funding availability that altered the council's capital strategy within the fiscal year.
findings.figures: Additional Investments February 2026 Council: £65.139m (appears to fund Direct Delivery Schemes totalling £530.099m across all years)
findings.quote: Additional Investments February 2026 Council 65.139 65.139

findings.headline: £10.053m of capital schemes slipped from 2025/26 into future years
findings.detail: Multiple capital projects deferred: A595 Grizebeck Stage 2 (£1.239m), Carriageway Future Programme (£1.116m), Bridges and Structures (£0.546m), and eleven smaller schemes. No single project failed catastrophically, but the pattern across diverse infrastructure (roads, flood resilience, property maintenance, disabled facility grants) suggests systemic delivery constraints.
findings.matters: Slippage reduces outturn against budget and can signal project management challenges, funding delays, or delivery constraints that affect the council's ability to execute its capital strategy.
findings.figures: Total Slippage Outturn 2025/26: (10.053m), slipped to 2026/27. Individual items range from £0.263m to £1.383m.

findings.paper_title: WFC 30/07 Capital Programme Update & Treasury Management 2025/26 Outturn Report
findings.headline: Treasury Management underspend of £6.300m is driven by £3.291m one-off saving from temporarily elevated interest rates on cash holdings.
findings.detail: The council achieved a £6.300m underspend in Treasury Management, of which £3.291m is explicitly identified as a one-off saving arising from high interest rates on the council's short-term cash balances. This benefit depends on interest rates remaining relatively high and is therefore temporary.
findings.matters: One-off treasury gains mask the underlying financial position; if interest rates fall, the council will face a corresponding loss of income that was offsetting other budget pressures.
findings.figures: Treasury Management underspend: £6.300m; One-off interest saving: £3.291m (2025/26 only)
findings.quote: This budget included a one-off saving of £3.291m in 2025/26 only, arising from the increased interest received on the Council's short-term cash balances, achievable as interest rates have remained relatively high.

findings.paper_title: WFC 30/07 Capital Programme Update & Treasury Management 2025/26 Outturn Report
findings.headline: Capital programme shows £10.053m total slippage, with £4.014m of infrastructure projects delayed from 2025/26 into 2026/27.
findings.detail: Five infrastructure projects slipped from 2025/26 to 2026/27: A595 Grizebeck Stage 2 (£1.239m), Carriageway Future Programme (£1.116m), Barrow Emergency Act Travel (£0.595m), Bridges & Structures (£0.546m), and Carriageway PSD Treatments (£0.518m). These delays affect roads and bridges, core infrastructure assets.
findings.matters: Slippage indicates the council is not delivering its capital plans to schedule and raises questions about project management capacity and whether service resilience improvements will be delayed.
findings.figures: Total slippage £4.014m requiring Council approval; A595 Grizebeck: (£1.239m), Carriageway Programme: (£1.116m), Barrow Emergency Act: (£0.595m), Bridges & Structures: (£0.546m), Carriageway PSD: (£0.518m)
findings.quote: Slippage of £2.669m was approved by Cabinet, and slippage of £4.014m requires approval by Council (see Table 5).

findings.paper_title: WFC 30/07 Capital Programme Update & Treasury Management 2025/26 Outturn Report
findings.headline: Council is deliberately avoiding new borrowing, choosing instead to offset approved borrowing against short-term cash reserves.
findings.detail: The council holds approved borrowing capacity but has implemented a strategy to avoid taking new loans, instead using short-term cash reserves to offset what would otherwise require borrowing. The council holds £74.6m in temporary investments earning 4.07% average interest and £173.6m in existing debt at 3.7% average interest rate.
findings.matters: This strategy depends on maintaining adequate cash balances and is exposed to interest rate movements; lenders need to understand the sustainability of avoiding new borrowing and whether the council's liquidity is sufficient for its capital plans.
findings.figures: Debt portfolio: £173.6m at 3.7% average interest; Temporary investments: £74.6m at 4.07%; no new external borrowing in the year
findings.quote: No new external borrowing has been undertaken in the year, with the Council implementing its strategy to offset previously approved borrowing with short-term cash reserves rather than incurring borrowing costs on new loans.

findings.headline: External auditors issued a disclaimed opinion on the 2024/25 Statement of Accounts
findings.detail: The Audit Committee approved the 2024/25 Statement of Accounts and Annual Governance Statement in February 2026 despite Grant Thornton (the appointed external auditors) issuing a disclaimed opinion rather than a standard audit opinion. The committee's approval was based on other sources of assurance built up across the year, not a normal audit sign-off.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion indicates the external auditors could not provide assurance on the financial statements in the normal way, suggesting significant uncertainties or limitations in audit scope. This raises questions about financial reporting reliability that directly affect lender confidence and require explanation.
findings.quote: In February 2026, the Audit Committee approved the 2024/25 Statement of Accounts and Annual Governance Statement. In view of the External Auditors' disclaimed opinion, the Audit Committee's consideration and approval was based on other sources of assurance built up across the year.

findings.headline: Priority delivery programmes underperforming with multiple 2025/26 objectives undelivered or scope altered
findings.detail: The council describes 2025/26 as 'a year for discovery, identification & decision making' with implementation to follow in 2026/27. At the end of Q4 2025/26, a number of priority programme objectives have not been delivered or had scope altered. While governance has tightened under the new CEO, the pattern of undelivered objectives creates execution risk around whether planned benefits and savings will materialise.
findings.matters: Transformation programmes are typically relied upon to generate future savings and efficiency gains. Slippage and scope changes suggest the council may not realise expected financial benefits on planned timescale.
findings.figures: Number of priority programme objectives not delivered or altered in scope; 2025/26 designated as discovery/decision phase with implementation in 2026/27
findings.quote: At the end of the 25/26 financial year there are a number of priority programme objectives that have not been delivered, or the scope has been altered to ensure altered outcomes were achieved.

findings.headline: Adult social care Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards referral volumes rising with persistent recruitment challenges (risk score 20)
findings.detail: DoLS referral volumes continue to rise. While the council is clearing more caseload, the risk of legal challenge remains high. The council has faced difficulty recruiting Best Interests Assessors (BIAs) and is now relying on agency resource to manage demand. This represents both rising service demand and growing reliance on external staffing.
findings.matters: Rising DoLS referrals represent both growing service demand and potential legal liability. Agency staffing indicates tight internal capacity and adds cost to service delivery.
findings.figures: Referral volumes still rising; reliance on agency BIA resource
findings.quote: Referral volumes are still rising, and while we are clearing more caseload, the risk of challenge remains high. It remains difficult to recruit Best Interests Assessors (BIA) but agency resource has now been agreed.

findings.headline: SEND system deficit reduced to score 15 but remains uncertain pending complex government reform plan submission
findings.detail: Risk score reduced from 20 to 15 following government recognition of the national systemic nature of SEND deficits and publication of the White Paper (Every Child Achieving and Thriving). However, there remains uncertainty as to what proportion of the cumulative SEND deficit the government will write-off; this depends on the council submitting a complex SEND Reform Plan in Q1 2026/27. The council has reduced spend on Independent School Places through its Better Value plan.
findings.matters: SEND has been a persistent unfunded pressure on councils nationally. While government reform is underway, the outcome for this council depends on plan submission success and government policy decisions outside its control.
findings.figures: Risk score reduced from 20 to 15; reduction in Independent School Places spend through Better Value plan
findings.quote: The publication of the White Paper (Every Child Achieving and Thriving), SEND Reform consultation and guidance on applications for a HNB Stability Grant has allowed for a reduction in the likelihood of the risk arising, but there remains uncertainty as to the proportion of the cumulative deficit which could be written-off.

findings.headline: Major workforce restructuring underway with identified risk of inability to maintain statutory service delivery
findings.detail: The council has completed a voluntary redundancy scheme and implemented Phase 1 of Senior Leadership restructure. Further phases and service-led restructures are in development. The risk register explicitly identifies that the pace and scale of change may result in change fatigue, reduced engagement and loss of key skills. The council flags that this could impact its ability to consistently deliver statutory services, maintain safe operations and deliver required transformation.
findings.matters: Large-scale restructuring creates execution risk and service quality risk. The council's own assessment that workforce changes could impair statutory service delivery is a direct indicator of capacity constraints.
findings.figures: Voluntary redundancy scheme completed; Phase 1 Senior Leadership restructure implemented; further phases in development
findings.quote: There remains a risk that the pace and scale of change may result in change fatigue, reduced engagement and the loss of key skills where not effectively managed. This could impact the Council's ability to consistently deliver statutory services, maintain safe operations and deliver transformation.

findings.headline: DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) deficit growing with council liability for write-off uncertain and dependent on government policy
findings.detail: The DSG deficit is growing. While government reform changes (SEND Reform Plan, HNB Stability Grant) are in train for 2026/27 through 2028/29, there is explicit uncertainty as to what proportion of the cumulative DSG deficit will fall to the council. This depends on successful submission of a complex SEND Reform Plan in Q1 2026/27. The report notes over 30 schools currently hold cumulative DSG deficits.
findings.matters: The timing and scale of DSG deficit recovery is contingent on national government policy and the council's ability to submit a successful reform plan. This is a material contingent liability with timing risk.
findings.figures: DSG deficit growing; over 30 schools with cumulative DSG deficits; proportion council will bear depends on 2026/27 government decisions
findings.quote: The DSG deficit is growing and although there are changes in 2026/27 through to 2028/29, the balance at 31 March 2028 will, in some part, fall to the Council.

findings.headline: School system deficit of £4.820m as at 31 March 2026 with 46 schools in deficit, deteriorating mid-year
findings.detail: The draft outturn shows a total school deficit balance of £4.820m, an increase of £0.909m compared to Q3 (indicating mid-year deterioration). There are 46 schools in deficit. Finance review meetings have been held with 35 affected schools. The School Deficit Balance Policy has been strengthened and Finance notes of concern have been issued to schools.
findings.matters: School deficits represent unfunded liabilities that the council ultimately carries. The scale (£4.820m) and upward trajectory mid-year suggest the council underestimated school funding needs and now faces a growing commitment.
findings.figures: £4.820m school deficit at 31 March 2026; increase of £0.909m from Q3; 46 schools in deficit
findings.quote: Draft outturn is an overall school deficit balance £4.820m an increase of £0.909m compared to Q3. There are 46 schools in deficit as at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Financial sustainability at critical risk (score 25) with £6m Q3 overspend and structural deficits persisting into future years
findings.detail: The council forecast a £6m overspend to 31 March 2026 in Q3. The S151 Officer has introduced new controls including weekly Spend Control Board reviewing all requests of £30k and above plus recruitment. Despite proposing a balanced budget for 2026/27, this requires significant savings and large deficits remain to be addressed in future years. The Medium-Term Financial Plan and reserves position are explicitly identified as high risks to future sustainability.
findings.matters: Structural overspends and forward-year deficits indicate the council's recurrent spending exceeds sustainable revenue. A lender needs confidence that the council can operate within its means; dependence on one-off reserves or unproven savings is a lending risk.
findings.figures: £6m overspend forecast Q3 2026; 2026/27 budget requires significant savings; large deficits in future years
findings.quote: The Q3 budget forecast was c£6m overspend for 31 March 2026... Large deficits remain to be addressed in future years.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing from £281.6m (2026/27) to £336m (2030/31)
findings.detail: The council's underlying borrowing need is expanding across the forecast period, reflecting continued capital investment. The CFR will grow by 19% over five years, increasing the long-term debt burden.
findings.matters: A growing CFR indicates increasing reliance on long-term borrowing to fund capital assets, with implications for intergenerational equity and long-term affordability.
findings.figures: General Fund CFR rises from £269.315m to £326.996m; Total borrowing need rises from £281.623m to £336.038m

findings.headline: £15m loans maturing in 2026/27 requiring refinancing at potentially higher rates
findings.detail: Significant debt maturity in the coming year will need to be refinanced. The timing and rates at which this is refinanced will depend on market conditions and the council's borrowing decisions.
findings.matters: Maturing debt must be refinanced, and depending on interest rates at refinancing, this could increase the council's annual debt service costs significantly.
findings.figures: £15.0m of loans maturing during 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council has loans of £15.0m maturing during 2026/27 and this is expected to be replaced with new borrowing.

findings.headline: Council maintaining under-borrowed position by drawing down £102.3m cash balances instead of external borrowing
findings.detail: Rather than externalising borrowing, the council is running down temporary cash reserves to finance capital and revenue needs. This defers costs but limits financial resilience and flexibility when cash runs low or when interest rates make deferral uneconomic.
findings.matters: This strategy temporarily reduces debt costs but exposes the council to interest rate risk and constrains flexibility if cash balances deplete faster than forecast.
findings.figures: £102.3m of cash balances projected to be used in lieu of external borrowing as at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: It is projected that as at 31 March 2026 c. £102.3m of cash balances will be used in lieu of external borrowing.

findings.headline: Capital programme of £122.6m in 2026/27 with £25.4m financed by prudential borrowing
findings.detail: The council plans substantial capital expenditure, with nearly a quarter to be financed through new borrowing. This drives the underlying capital financing requirement and future debt servicing costs.
findings.matters: The scale of capital plans determines future borrowing needs and debt service obligations, which directly affects the council's financial capacity.
findings.figures: £122.637m total capital expenditure; £25.4m prudential borrowing in 2026/27
findings.quote: Estimates of proposed capital expenditure... Total 122.637 [£m]... Estimates of proposed capital expenditure funded by prudential borrowing... 25.400 [£m]

findings.headline: Financing costs rising to 6.78% of revenue by 2030/31, up from 4.02% in 2026/27
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream increases materially over the five-year forecast period. This reduces the council's financial flexibility and constrains the resources available for service delivery, as an increasing share of revenue must service borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how much of the council's revenue is consumed by debt service, and this trajectory shows significant fiscal tightening ahead.
findings.quote: Ratio of Finance costs to Net Revenue Stream 4.02% 5.30% 6.08% 6.44% 6.78%

findings.headline: External audit flagged DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) deficit as a key issue; capacity constraints also identified across multiple external assessments
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's 2024/25 audit highlighted a DSG deficit, governance improvements still needed, and capacity constraints. CQC assessed Adult Social Care as 'Requires Improvement' (score 62/100), citing service performance impacted by 'delays, provision and capacity constraints'. LGA Corporate Peer Review called for 'sharper focus, faster delivery and stronger organisational grip'.
findings.matters: A DSG deficit is a specific unfunded liability. Consistent feedback on capacity from three independent external assessors suggests genuine resource constraints affecting service delivery and financial stability.
findings.figures: CQC score 62/100 (requires improvement); DSG deficit not quantified
findings.quote: Grant Thornton (External Audit) – Annual Audit Report 2024/25 (February 2026) – concluded Council had strong foundations, stable finances, good governance arrangements and positive service performance in key areas. However, highlighted key issues in terms of DSG deficit, improving governance, capacity in some areas and performance management

findings.headline: Financial system complexity persists: consolidated from 5 legacy ledgers to 1, but feeder system interfaces still require simplification
findings.detail: By 31 March 2026, the council retired all legacy financial ledgers to a single ledger system. However, Internal Audit notes work is 'ongoing to simplify feeder system interfaces', indicating the underlying architecture remains complex and potentially fragile.
findings.matters: Complex feeder systems increase risk of data errors, delays in financial reporting, and operational disruption. Unfinished system work suggests the finance function is not yet optimised.
findings.figures: Consolidated from 5 to 1 financial ledger effective 1 April 2026
findings.quote: The move from five to one financial ledger will support greater internal control although work is ongoing to simplify feeder system interfaces.

findings.headline: High concentration of strategic risks: 10 of 16 risks rated as 'high' by Quarter 3, up from 8 of 17 in Quarter 1
findings.detail: The council's strategic risk register deteriorated through the year, with the proportion of high-rated risks increasing. Risk Appetite Statement and Risk Framework remain incomplete and are only now being finalised (due to CMT for July 2026). This suggests risk governance frameworks lag behind risk exposure.
findings.matters: 62% of strategic risks at high severity indicates the council is managing substantial operational challenges. A lender would need to understand which specific risks these are and whether management frameworks are adequate.
findings.figures: Q1: 8 high out of 17 total risks; Q3: 10 high out of 16 total risks
findings.quote: The 2025/26 Quarter 1 Strategic Risk Report and Risk Register for Westmorland and Furness Council contained 17 strategic risks identified as relevant to the operation of the Council, with 8 risks rated as high and 9 rated as medium. By Quarter 3 of 2025/26 there were 16 strategic risks identified as relevant to the operation of the Council, with 10 risks rated as high and 6 rated as medium.

findings.headline: 23% of completed risk-based audits received only partial assurance; one multi-year issue (Business Continuity) remains unresolved
findings.detail: Of 26 completed audits, 6 resulted in partial assurance ratings (23%), meaning weaknesses were identified that could place achievement of objectives at risk. A follow-up review of Business Continuity Planning remains at partial assurance despite previous audit, suggesting slow remediation pace.
findings.matters: Multiple partial assurance ratings indicate control deficiencies across operational areas. Slow progress on follow-ups suggests the council struggles to remediate audit findings in a timely way.
findings.figures: 6 out of 26 audits (23%) partial assurance; 20 out of 26 (77%) reasonable or substantial
findings.quote: Of the 26 risk based audits (excludes schools) completed, or at draft report stage, 20 received reasonable or substantial assurance (77%), whilst 6 resulted in partial assurance (23%).

findings.headline: Significant payments being made without purchase orders; external audit flagged this, remediation planned for 2026/27
findings.detail: External audit identified a material control weakness: many payments are processed without corresponding purchase orders. Management is developing a 'No PO No pay' policy but has not yet implemented it. Implementation will be considered as part of accounts payable work in 2026/27, meaning the control gap persists through at least March 2027.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled payments increase fraud and error risk. A lender would need confidence in payables controls; a multi-year gap before remediation is concerning.
findings.figures: Not quantified in report; described as 'significant number'
findings.quote: The issue of a significant number of payments being made without a corresponding purchase order was highlighted by external audit. Management are currently looking at this issues and plan to introduce a policy of 'No purchase order (PO) No pay'. The implementation of this will be considered as part of our work on accounts payable in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: CAB 17/03 - 2025/26 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring report to 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves are being drawn down with £1.071m used in Q3 for immediate pressures
findings.detail: Q3 drew £1.071m from earmarked reserves: Enabler Services £0.673m for ICT programme, Resources £0.382m for Housing Benefit settlement, Thriving Places £0.016m for grant matching. Net projected reserves position at 31 March 2026 is (£34.586m) with gross reserves (£71.497m).
findings.matters: Ongoing drawdowns of earmarked reserves reduce financial flexibility and shock-absorption capacity, indicating the council is using reserves to manage operational pressures rather than fund strategic investments.
findings.figures: Q3 draws £1.071m (Enabler £0.673m, Resources £0.382m); net reserves forecast (£34.586m); gross reserves (£71.497m)
findings.quote: During Quarter 3 £1.071m of earmarked reserves have been drawn down for: Thriving Places £0.016m; to match grant expenditure; Enabler £0.673m; ICT programme project expenditures; Resources £0.382m; Housing Benefit Subsidy claim settlement

findings.paper_title: CAB 17/03 - 2025/26 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring report to 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Treasury Management underspend of £5.564m is masking underlying operational pressures and depends on interest rates
findings.detail: The council is not undertaking new external borrowing in 2025/26, instead using short-term cash reserves to offset approved borrowing plans. This avoids £3.705m in borrowing costs. Higher-than-budgeted interest rates produce £2.286m additional income. Together this £5.564m underspend significantly masks the £11.349m directorate overspend.
findings.matters: The council's true operating position is worse than headline figures suggest. This financial relief is temporary and dependent on interest rate maintenance. If rates fall, the underlying £11.349m operational deficit will be exposed.
findings.figures: £5.564m Treasury Management underspend (£3.705m avoided borrowing, £2.286m additional interest); no new external borrowing undertaken
findings.quote: No new external borrowing has been undertaken in the first nine months of 2025/26, with the Council implementing its strategy to offset previously approved borrowing with short term cash reserves rather than incurring borrowing costs on new loans. This strategy has generated £3.705m savings in the year.

findings.paper_title: CAB 17/03 - 2025/26 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring report to 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Adult and Children's Services forecast demand-driven overspends of £4.926m and £5.111m respectively
findings.detail: Adult Services forecasts £4.926m overspend with Residential & Nursing Care £4.327m, Home Care £3.001m, and Supported Living £1.150m pressures, reflecting continued high demand. Children's Services forecasts £5.111m overspend with Cared for Children demand £2.075m, SEND transport £1.835m (driven by 21 net new pupils in 2025/26), and Home to School transport £0.858m (higher than 2024/25 demand).
findings.matters: Growing statutory demand for social care and education services that the council cannot control represents a major structural budget pressure that will recur annually unless the council reduces placements or the government changes funding.
findings.figures: Adult Services: Residential/Nursing £4.327m, Home Care £3.001m, Supported Living £1.150m; Children's: Cared for Children £2.075m, SEND transport £1.835m, Home to School transport £0.858m
findings.quote: Demand fluctuates but remains high for Residential and Nursing Care, Home Care and Supported Living, with respective forecast variances of £4.327m, £3.001m and £1.150m.

findings.paper_title: CAB 17/03 - 2025/26 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring report to 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Agency staffing costs are significant and persistent across Adult Services, Child Protection and Waste
findings.detail: Adult Services Older Adults forecasts £2.023m pressure driven by 'the use of costly agency staff to fill vacancies and cover sickness.' Child Protection has £0.691m pressure from 'continued reliance on agency workers to cover vacancies and maternity leave.' Waste Services has £0.913m agency cost pressure. This pattern indicates the council cannot recruit or retain permanent staff in front-line statutory services.
findings.matters: Persistent agency staffing is costly and indicates deeper recruitment and retention challenges that may affect service delivery quality and sustainability.
findings.figures: £2.023m Older Adults staffing pressures; £0.691m Child Protection agency; £0.913m Waste Services agency costs
findings.quote: In Older Adults, the predicted deficit of £2.023m is driven by staffing pressures, with the use of costly agency staff to fill vacancies and cover sickness.

findings.paper_title: CAB 17/03 - 2025/26 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring report to 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Approved savings of £11.045m are delivering only £9.634m, with £1.411m undelivered
findings.detail: The council's transformation savings programme is underperforming. Adults Promoting Independence diagnostic (£1.000m) is undeliverable due to delays. Children's Home to School Transport saving (£0.100m) is not delivering as demand increases offset savings. Staff Turnover vacancy saving (£0.311m of £0.600m plan) is failing as vacancies are covered by agency staff rather than left unfilled.
findings.matters: Undelivered savings indicate the council's transformation programme is not progressing as planned. This adds to the year-end deficit and signals challenges in executing strategic change.
findings.figures: £1.411m total shortfall: Adults Promoting Independence £1.000m, Children's transport £0.100m, Staff Turnover £0.311m of £0.600m plan
findings.quote: Adults Promoting Independence – Diagnostic (£1.000m): undeliverable in 2025/26 due to delays commencing the initial diagnostic work. No alternatives have been proposed to mitigate this.

findings.paper_title: CAB 17/03 - 2025/26 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring report to 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has grown to £34.775m, driven by rising SEN demand
findings.detail: The cumulative DSG deficit is forecast at £34.775m by March 2026 (up from £22.135m brought forward). The High Needs Block alone is £40.143m in deficit. The in-year pressure deteriorated by £0.891m from Q2 to £12.640m. Growth in EHCPs is the driver: 2,692 children as at 31 December 2025, representing 8.5% growth since March 2025. The council's EHCP rate exceeds national and statistical neighbour averages.
findings.matters: This represents a structural, recurring deficit that the statutory override currently separates from general reserves but which signals growing unfunded statutory demand that will require either government funding confirmation or future council funding solution.
findings.figures: £34.775m cumulative DSG deficit; High Needs £40.143m deficit; in-year pressure £12.640m (£0.891m worse than Q2); 2,692 EHCPs (+8.5% since March 2025)
findings.quote: The number of children and young people with an EHCP as at 31 December 2025 is 2,692; an increase of 8.5% since March 2025.

findings.paper_title: CAB 17/03 - 2025/26 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring report to 31 December 2025
findings.headline: Revenue budget forecast to overspend by £5.839m despite management actions
findings.detail: The council's revised budget is £307.271m but forecast outturn is £313.110m. While this represents a £4.134m improvement from Q2's £9.973m overspend, the council states that 'additional mitigations are required to reach a balanced budget for 2025/26.' The overspend reflects £11.349m directorate pressures partially offset by a £5.564m Treasury Management underspend.
findings.matters: An unresolved year-end overspend indicates operational spending exceeds available resources and will require either emergency service cuts or drawdown of reserves to achieve budget closure.
findings.figures: £5.839m overspend on £307.271m budget; improved from £9.973m at Q2 but £4.154m mitigation already achieved
findings.quote: The forecast net expenditure position as at 31 December 2025 (Q3) is £313.110m, compared to the revised net budget of £307.271m. This is a forecast overspend of £5.839m.

findings.headline: Collection Fund deficits of £3.485m (£2.025m Council Tax + £1.460m Business Rates) in 2026/27
findings.detail: Council Tax deficit driven by reduction in premiums, increase in single person discounts, and increase in exemptions/reductions. Business Rates deficit from rateable value changes following Valuation Office challenges and appeals. These are one-off hits to the budget that reduce available funds.
findings.matters: Collection fund deficits reduce in-year cash available and must be covered from reserves or other sources, adding to reserve depletion.
findings.figures: £2.025m Council Tax deficit; £1.460m Business Rates deficit; £3.485m total
findings.quote: The Collection Fund deficit for Council Tax in the 2026/27 budget is £2.025m and this is a largely a result of a reduction in premiums, an increase in single person discounts, and an increase in exemptions and reductions.

findings.headline: Government Council Tax assumptions overstate realistic growth by £5m-£15.7m across the planning period
findings.detail: Government assumes 2.9% annual Council Tax base growth in Core Spending Power calculations, but realistic local growth is 0.7%. This creates an additional underfunding of £5m in 2026/27, rising to £15.7m by 2028/29. The document suggests if the double count of the Second Homes Premium growth had been corrected, the council should have received a funding floor payment. This is a material systematic underestimation of the council's true funding position.
findings.matters: The council's published funding settlement materially overstates available resources; this amplifies the effective funding cut and makes recovery harder.
findings.figures: £5m understatement 2026/27; £15.7m by 2028/29; government assumes 2.9% growth vs. realistic 0.7%
findings.quote: The Core Spending Power overstates Council Tax income by £5m for 2026/27 as that Taxbase is calculated and known, and the overstatement increases to £15.7m by 2028/29.

findings.headline: Public Health Grant of £8.8m is only £38.84 per capita vs. £73.90 England average; 47% below national average
findings.detail: Westmorland receives £8.8m (2025/26), equating to £38.84 per capita, against an England average of £73.90 and CIPFA comparator average of £57.10. Over 80% is committed to mandated functions (health visiting, sexual health, drug/alcohol treatment, smoking cessation). Non-mandated services receive under £300k (under 3% of total). The council operates at 'minimum viable' level of public health provision with limited capacity for prevention, early intervention, or meeting inequalities.
findings.matters: Chronic underfunding of public health translates to higher long-term demand on social care, health, and criminal justice; a lender should factor this into population health trajectory and medium-term demand pressures.
findings.figures: £8.8m 2025/26; £38.84 per capita vs £73.90 national average; 47% below average; 80% committed to mandated functions
findings.quote: Westmorland and Furness receiving £8.8m in 2025/26, equating to just £38.84 per capita, compared with an England average of £73.90...Without a material increase in PHG funding, the authority will continue to operate at a 'minimum viable' level of public health provision, with limited scope to meet rising need, address inequalities, or deliver the full breadth of statutory duties.

findings.headline: Schools in deficit: 34 schools with combined deficit of £7.656m; forecast to worsen to £3.911m net deficit by March 2026
findings.detail: Maintained schools reported net deficit of £2.136m at March 2025, deteriorating by £2.586m from prior year. This is driven by falling pupil numbers, unsustainable staffing structures, rising staffing costs, and SEND pressures. The council is conducting finance reviews with 31 schools; follow-up reviews scheduled for Spring 2026 but no resolution strategy yet articulated.
findings.matters: School deficits are a liability the council must ultimately absorb or allow to accumulate. Continued deterioration suggests structural overspend in education, which diverts resources from elsewhere.
findings.figures: 34 schools in deficit; combined total £7.656m; net deficit forecast £3.911m by 31 March 2026
findings.quote: At 31 March 2025, maintained schools reported a net deficit of £2.136m, a deterioration of £2.586m from the previous year...Based on October 2025 budget plans, the net deficit is forecast to increase further to £3.911m by 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Large savings programme (£30.9m) with multiple delivery and consultation risks not yet resolved
findings.detail: The council proposes savings across workforce (£5.1m redundancies, voluntary scheme), parking income (£0.9m via 10% charge increase), garden waste subscription (£1.6m via £60 annual charge), carers direct payments cuts (£0.06m reducing from £1,500 to £400), leisure and culture cuts (£0.7m), and others. Many items require consultation or face uptake/delivery risk. Failure to realise savings would worsen the 2027/28 deficit immediately.
findings.matters: Savings programmes of this scale carry execution risk; if uptake of new charges is poor or consultation on service cuts delays implementation, the deficits widen and reserve drawdown accelerates.
findings.figures: £30.9m total savings; £5.092m workforce; £1.540m procurement; £1.760m second homes reductions; £3.191m Thriving Places; £0.671m Thriving Communities
findings.quote: The Council has developed a comprehensive savings programme totalling £30.9m and proposes the use of £3m of reserves and £3m of provisions in order to achieve a balanced budget for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Government funding cut by £43m by 2028/29 due to Fair Funding Review removal of remoteness adjustment
findings.detail: Compared to the existing MTFP, funding reduces by £12m in 2026/27, rising to £27m in 2027/28 and £43m in 2028/29. The removal of the Rural Services Delivery Grant (£6.5m historically) and removal of remoteness weighting in the Area Cost Adjustment (£17.4m impact) are permanent structural cuts. Westmorland is the most sparsely populated upper-tier LA in England, making this especially damaging.
findings.matters: Permanent reduction in government support means the council cannot expect baseline funding to recover; this is structural deficiency, not cyclical, requiring permanent service cuts.
findings.figures: £12m 2026/27; £27m 2027/28; £43m 2028/29; £6.5m Rural Services Delivery Grant withdrawn; £17.4m remoteness adjustment removed
findings.quote: The Review removes rurality and remoteness adjustments and consolidates grant streams, resulting in a substantial loss of core funding for Westmorland and Furness. Compared to the existing Medium-Term Financial Plan, this equates to a £12m reduction in 2026/27, rising to £27m in 2027/28 and reaching £43m by 2028/29.

findings.headline: Section 151 Officer assesses council as high-risk with potential need for Exceptional Financial Support from Government
findings.detail: The Director of Resources explicitly warns that the scale of uncertainty, demand pressures, and future unfunded deficits could necessitate exceptional financial support from Government if adverse conditions worsen or if planned savings fail to materialise. This is an unusually stark assessment of distress.
findings.matters: This is a formal warning from the council's chief finance officer that the council's financial position may become unsustainable, raising material refinancing risk.
findings.figures: None; qualitative assessment
findings.quote: The Section 151 Officer assesses the Council's financial position as high-risk, warning that the scale of uncertainty, demand pressures and future unfunded deficits could necessitate Exceptional Financial Support from Government if adverse conditions worsen or if planned savings fail to materialise.

findings.headline: High Needs Block DSG deficit rising to £62m by 2028; statutory override ends, creating major unfunded risk
findings.detail: The council has a projected cumulative high needs deficit of £39.068m at Q2 2025/26, rising to £62m by 2028. The statutory override that allows DSG deficits to be ring-fenced ends in 2028. Government has pledged to cover 90% of historic deficit accrued to end 2025/26, but future arrangements are unconfirmed. If the council is required to absorb any portion locally post-2028, this creates a potential £10-20m liability.
findings.matters: This is a crystallised, quantifiable future liability. If the override ends and the council must absorb deficits, this could force service cuts or require external intervention.
findings.figures: £39.068m cumulative deficit Q2 2025/26; £62m projected by 2028; government pledges to cover 90% of historic deficit
findings.quote: The DSG statutory override was extended until March 2028 because of the national issues in respect of the High Needs deficit positions. In the final Local Government Finance Settlement, government have pledged to cover 90% of the historic deficit accrued up to the end of 2025/26...Councils await formal confirmation of the arrangements from government.

findings.headline: Reserves forecast to fall from £46.1m to £22.4m by 2028, reducing financial resilience
findings.detail: The council is drawing down reserves to balance the current year (£6m total use in 2026/27), and the Medium-Term Financial Plan projects reserves will fall by half over three years to £22.4m by 2028. This assumes no mitigation of the 2027/28 gap, leaving minimal buffer for unexpected pressures or service failures.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves weakens the council's ability to absorb demand shocks, service failures, or further funding reductions, increasing default or restructuring risk.
findings.figures: £46.1m at end 2025/26; forecast £22.4m by 2028
findings.quote: Overall, reserves are forecast to fall from £46.1m at the end of 2025/26 to £22.4m by 2028, excluding the Housing Revenue Account and DSG balances; this assumes that the budget gap in 2027/28 is not mitigated or reduced.

findings.headline: Structural budget deficits of £16.3m and £32.8m remain unresolved in 2027/28 and 2028/29 despite £30.9m savings plan
findings.detail: The council balances 2026/27 through £3m of reserves and £3m of provisions, but the underlying structural budget gaps persist into the medium term. The document states 'a great deal of work is required to bring 2027/28 and future years into balance' with no solutions yet identified. This moves the crisis forward rather than solving it.
findings.matters: Unresolved structural deficits indicate the council's financial model is not sustainable; reserves are being used to defer rather than solve the problem, which raises refinancing risk.
findings.figures: £36.9m budget gap closed with £30.9m savings, £3m reserves, £3m provisions; £16.3m gap 2027/28; £32.8m gap 2028/29
findings.quote: Although this balances the coming year, significant structural budget gaps of £16.3m in 2027/28 and £32.8m in 2028/29 remain unresolved.

findings.headline: Collection fund deficit of £3.486m built into the 2026/27 requirement
findings.detail: The council is recovering a £3.486m collection fund deficit through the 2026/27 council tax, rather than absorbing it from reserves. The council reports a 99% collection rate, suggesting the deficit reflects prior-year budget variance rather than collection failure.
findings.matters: A deficit being passed through to council tax indicates either prior-year overspending not covered by reserves, or a deliberate choice not to use reserves, both of which signal tighter financial position.
findings.figures: Collection fund deficit £3.486m; collection rate 99%
findings.quote: Plus the Collection Fund Deficit 3.486

findings.headline: Budget figures remain provisional pending completion of Local Government Reorganisation stabilisation work
findings.detail: The council explicitly flags that its gross budget of £640.22m is only 'our best estimate' as budget elements are still being examined post-reorganization. This is stated at the point where the budget is being formally approved, indicating material uncertainty.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director needs to know whether these figures are firm commitments or subject to material change, particularly given this is a newly formed authority still working through reorganization impacts.
findings.figures: Gross expenditure £640,222,068.17 (noted as provisional)
findings.quote: the gross budget is our best estimate as we continue to examine some budget elements as part of the Local Government Reorganisation stabilisation work

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for AC - Audit Findings Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Multiple control policy gaps identified: no formal redundancy approval policy in place until August 2025; property title registration incomplete
findings.detail: A £100k+ voluntary redundancy exit was paid in May 2025 without documented formal prior approval, only retrospective approval in August 2025, due to absence of a post-LGR redundancy policy. Additionally, several properties have unsigned conveyances but remain unregistered at Land Registry.
findings.matters: Missing or retrospective approvals for major payments and unregistered properties indicate weak control environments and title risks. Governance control failures can lead to loss of assets or improper payments.
findings.figures: Exit package over £100k; multiple unregistered properties
findings.quote: Our review of remuneration disclosures identified that a Voluntary Redundancy exit with total cost over £100k was not subject to documented formal approval prior to payment in May 2025. We understand this occurred due to the lack of a Voluntary Redundancy policy following LGR.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for AC - Audit Findings Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Legacy Barrow Council ledger reconciliation unresolved; disaggregation of opening balances from prior year has no audit assurance
findings.detail: Following 2023-24 local government reorganization, the council disaggregated Cumbria County Council closing balances to create opening balances for 2024-25. The auditors have not been able to reconcile the Barrow legacy ledger to the primary E5 general ledger due to unresolved variances. Additionally, prior year 2023-24 accounts received a full disclaimer, meaning no assurance exists over opening balances.
findings.matters: Unresolved reconciliations mean the council cannot demonstrate that legacy balances were correctly transferred post-LGR. Without audit assurance over opening balances, closing reserves cannot be verified.
findings.figures: Not quantified; relates to multiple legacy councils (Eden, South Lakeland, Barrow, and waste service assets valued at £19.0m)
findings.quote: We have not been able to complete our procedures to verify the complete and accurate transfer of transaction data from the Barrow Council legacy ledger due to some unresolved variances and we have not obtained sufficient evidence to demonstrate the legacy ledger data reconciles to the journals posted into the primary E5 general ledger.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for AC - Audit Findings Report 2024/25
findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting substantially revised during audit, suggesting poor initial assessment; additional £6.5m lease liabilities identified
findings.detail: The council initially recorded IFRS 16 lease liabilities of £1.279m and ROU assets of £1.452m. Following further review by management in response to auditor inquiries, revised working papers increased lease liabilities by £6.5m and ROU assets by £5.8m. Auditors have outstanding queries on lease calculations and peppercorn leases.
findings.matters: A five-fold increase in lease liabilities discovered during audit suggests the council's initial IFRS 16 implementation was incomplete or inaccurate, with potential for further adjustments.
findings.figures: Initial: £1.279m liabilities, £1.452m ROU assets; Revised: additional £6.5m liabilities, additional £5.8m ROU assets
findings.quote: Management carried out a further review of IFRS16 and we received revised working papers to support the Council's assessment of lease liabilities and right of use assets on 15 December. This included additional lease liabilities of £6.5m and additional Right of Use Assets of £5.8m which has been adjusted in the updated accounts.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for AC - Audit Findings Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Expenditure control weaknesses: £0.3m year-end error missed by accruals process; £49.8m non-Purchase Order expenditure in three months
findings.detail: Auditors identified a £0.3m invoice for 2024-25 expenditure that was not processed as a Purchase Order and was missed in year-end accruals, only found when invoice arrived post year-end. Additionally, the council processed £49.8m of non-Purchase Order expenditure in the three-month period March-May 2025, creating extended audit testing requirements.
findings.matters: Significant volumes of non-PO expenditure create risk of uncontrolled spending and unmatched liabilities. The missed accrual shows the council's year-end close process is not reliable.
findings.figures: £0.3m; £49.8m non-PO expenditure in 3 months (Mar-May 2025)
findings.quote: Our substantive testing of invoices received after the year end identified an error in relation to an invoice of £0.3m related to 2024-25 expenditure which was recorded in the following financial year in error...The Council transacts a significant volume of non-Purchase Order expenditure with invoices totalling £49.8m in the 3 months March to May 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for AC - Audit Findings Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Revenue recognition audit procedures incomplete; grant income conditions and clawback risks not fully assessed
findings.detail: Auditors could not fully conclude substantive testing of revenue. They obtained sample evidence for grant income but were unable to verify whether all conditions associated with grants had been satisfied or whether grants carried clawback risk. Additional queries on fees and charges transactions remained unresolved.
findings.matters: Incomplete testing of revenue means the council's income base has not been fully verified by auditors, creating uncertainty over the completeness and accuracy of income statements.
findings.figures: Not quantified in excerpt
findings.quote: We have not been able to fully conclude our substantive testing of revenue. We have agreed a sample of grant income to supporting documentation to verify the occurrence, however, we have not obtained sufficient and appropriate evidence to demonstrate whether any conditions associated with grant income have been fully satisfied or give rise to any liability for clawback of funding.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for AC - Audit Findings Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Investment property misstatement of £0.856m and unresolved £3m provision for hosted services costs not recorded
findings.detail: Auditors identified that investment property was misstated due to outdated lease documentation and wrong asset classification, resulting in a net understatement of £0.856m. Separately, a £3m provision for additional hosted services costs was included but auditors could not obtain sufficient evidence that management's assumptions were reasonable or that the provision met accounting framework criteria.
findings.matters: The £3m provision remains in draft accounts as an unadjusted misstatement, meaning reserves may be overstated by that amount. Investment property errors suggest valuation control weaknesses.
findings.figures: £0.856m understatement (investment property); £3m provision for hosted services
findings.quote: We have identified that a provision for £3m is included in the draft accounts in relation to additional costs for hosted services however, we have not obtained sufficient evidence to demonstrate management's assumption is reasonable or that this meets the criteria in the financial reporting framework to recognise a provision.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for AC - Audit Findings Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Auditors identified significant weaknesses in council's VFM arrangements and are not satisfied on economy, efficiency and effectiveness
findings.detail: The auditors completed their Value for Money work and identified significant weaknesses in the council's arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in use of resources. A separate Auditor's Annual Report sets out detailed findings on governance, financial sustainability, and efficiency.
findings.matters: VFM concerns from external auditors flag systemic issues in how the council operates its finances and manages resources - relevant to repayment capacity and financial management risk.
findings.figures: Not specified in detail in this extract
findings.quote: We identified significant weaknesses in the Council's arrangements and so are not satisfied that the Council has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 for AC - Audit Findings Report 2024/25
findings.headline: Auditor will disclaim opinion for the second consecutive year, unable to complete audit by statutory deadline
findings.detail: Grant Thornton stopped the 2024-25 audit in January 2026 and will not complete sufficient procedures before the 27 February 2026 backstop deadline. This follows a full disclaimer of opinion in 2023-24. The council has no assurance over opening balances from the prior year and multiple material audit areas remain incomplete.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means financial statements cannot be relied on. Two consecutive years of disclaimers signals underlying control or evidence management problems that suggest financial reporting risk.
findings.figures: Statutory backstop deadline 27 February 2026; audit stopped week commencing 5 January 2026
findings.quote: As we have agreed with officers that we will not complete the audit for 2024-25 and the fact that the previous year's audit was subject to backstop-related disclaimed audit opinions, we have been unable to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion

news_drafts.headline: Large accountable-body capital programmes (externally delivered schemes) adding £49.451m outturn
news_drafts.lead: Reliance on external delivery creates exposure to third-party project delays and funding conditions outside direct council control.

news_drafts.headline: £65.139m in additional capital investments added mid-year in February 2026
news_drafts.lead: Mid-year addition of this scale indicates either unbudgeted capital needs or a change in funding availability that altered the council's capital strategy within the fiscal year.

news_drafts.headline: £10.053m of capital schemes slipped from 2025/26 into future years
news_drafts.lead: Slippage reduces outturn against budget and can signal project management challenges, funding delays, or delivery constraints that affect the council's ability to execute its capital strategy.
